This is one of the worst games you can play with your partner.

Spoilers!
What kind of parents, when faced with a problem, immediately choose to hurt their own children?

The part with the plushie toy genuinely hurt me. Every time something happened, I kept saying, "Nooo, they're probably going to learn from this and become better people." They didn't. Not even by the end.

There was no real character development. It all felt forced rather than genuine. The gameplay itself is pretty okay, but that doesn't make up for the horrible story and the characters.

And I understand that they're supposed to represent a dysfunctional family, but still... Even at the end, they were just as awful and dysfunctional as before. Honestly, I don't think getting a divorce would be such a bad idea in their case.

It Takes Two is a charming and enjoyable co-op adventure that's best experienced with a close friend or partner. The game offers a great variety of creative puzzles, platforming challenges, and unique gameplay mechanics that encourage cooperation and teamwork.

I'm particularly impressed with how well-balanced the difficulty is. It's neither too easy nor overly challenging, making it accessible to casual players while still being engaging enough for experienced gamers.

Overall, it's a well-designed, polished, and memorable co-op experience that's easy to recommend, especially if you have someone special to share the adventure with.

The game teaches you that adults can be assholes and selfish ([spoiler]the elephant scene, anyone?[/spoiler]) and that the true victims of divorce are the children. In fact, Rose proves to be more mature than the two of them combined, making her the true hero of the game.

This was consistently one of the top recommendations for games to play with your partner, so I picked it up on sale and played two sessions, at a little over three hours each, with my fiancée.

Not exceptional, but good, definitely!

The issue I have is that this is a story-driven game (story being the product of characters) with some of the least likeable characters I've had to endure:

Nearly everything out of a character's mouth is either mind-numbingly stupid or overtly cringey.
Either whomever wrote the dialogue has no respect for their audience or they simply need to improve their craft.

It's all so on-the-nose and lazy. It feels like a YA or straight up children's television level of character choices, expository dialogue, and unfunny jokes, but supposedly dealing with adult themes of long-term romantic love and the changes to a relationship that happen along the way.

A great premise poorly executed by bad writing; only a problem because of how story-centric the game actually is.

★ ★ ★ ★ ☆ → 4.5 out of 5 stars

One of those games that really shows how much better gaming can be when you have the right person playing with you. Its a duo game through & through and honestly, your experience depends quite a bit on who youre playing with.

The visuals are fantastic, every chapter has its own identity and the dialogue is genuinely well written. Took us roughly 15 hours to finish and theres a surprising amount of variety throughout.

I also really liked how the story approaches divorce and how much it can affect a child. 
Rose's perspective adds a lot more weight to the adventure than you might initially expect. 
And of course, Dr. Hakim is an absolute highlight, haha

The gameplay itself isn't particularly difficult. It's more about getting into a flow, working together and enjoying the ride rather than sitting there trying to solve overly complicated puzzles.

My only real complaint was the occasional scripting bug. Since certain sections rely on scripted sequences to progress, we sometimes had to replay parts of a level because an event simply didn't trigger, even though we had completed everything correctly. Nothing game breaking but definitely frustrating when it happens.

Overall, a fantastic co op experience. 
Definitely one I'd recommend playing with someone you enjoy spending time with! 


As Dr. Hakim would say:

"We are better together!"

[h1]It Takes Two — Couple's Therapy, With Unnecessary Elephant Trauma[/h1]

I'll admit it: I started It Takes Two sceptical.

My usual taste leans towards gritty, realistic, and often brutal games like GTA V, Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order and Survivor, and Detroit: Become Human. So, naturally, this colourful, cartoonish adventure looked like a bit of a departure from my usual gaming diet.

But this was the first co-op game I played with my fiancée, and I'm SO glad I gave it a chance.

[b]THE STORY — MORE THAN JUST A CUTE LITTLE ADVENTURE[/b]

Beneath its colourful art style lies a genuinely heartfelt story about a relationship that's been falling apart for years. It explores love, frustration, resentment, and the difficult process of finding your way back to someone.

What really stood out to both of us was the ending. It doesn't magically fix years of broken trust and accumulated problems just because two people spend a few hours working together. But it shows that those hours can be a beginning. A first step towards something better.

And honestly? That hit harder than I expected from a game featuring talking household objects.

[b]THE GAMEPLAY — TWO BRAINCELLS, ONE OBJECTIVE[/b]

The gameplay is an absolute blast. Every level introduces new mechanics, abilities, and challenges that constantly change how you and your partner need to cooperate. Just when you've mastered one set of mechanics, the game throws something completely different at you.

Communication matters, teamwork matters, and sometimes you will absolutely blame your partner for your own spectacular failure. It's practically relationship counselling with platforming.

And that upside-down section? No spoilers, but we had a great time with that one.

[b]THE ELEPHANT — I WANT A LAWYER[/b]

If you've played it, you know.

If you haven't, I'm not spoiling it.

All I'll say is that I went into this game expecting a wholesome co-op adventure, and I came out carrying emotional damage caused by an elephant.

[b]THE VERDICT[/b]

It Takes Two surprised me in the best possible way. The story is heartfelt, the gameplay constantly stays fresh, and sharing the experience with my fiancée made it all the more special.

You don't need to be a fan of colourful platformers. You don't even need to think this is your kind of game.

Just find someone you love, grab a second controller, and give it a chance.

[b]9/10. One point deducted for the elephant incident. I will never financially or emotionally recover.[/b]
